column4: A Look At The Fair Value Of Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM)
column10: [Key InsightsThe projected fair value for Waste Management is US$151 based on 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to EquityWith US$171 share price, Waste Management appears to be trading close to its estimated fair value Analyst price target for WM is US$175, which is 16% above our fair value estimateHow far off is Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM) from its intrinsic value? Using the most recent financial data, we'll take a look at whether the stock is fairly priced by taking the forecast future cash flows of the company and discounting them back to today's value. We will take advantage of the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model for this purpose. It may sound complicated, but actually it is quite simple!We generally believe that a company's value is the present value of all of the cash it will generate in the future. However, a DCF is just one valuation metric among many, and it is not without flaws. For those who are keen learners of equity analysis, the Simply Wall St analysis model here may be something of interest to you. Check out our latest analysis for Waste Management The ModelWe are going to use a two-stage DCF model, which, as the name states, takes into account two stages of growth. The first stage is generally a higher growth period which levels off heading towards the terminal value, captured in the second 'steady growth' period. To start off with, we need to estimate the next ten years of cash flows. Where possible we use analyst estimates, but when these aren't available we extrapolate the previous free cash flow (FCF) from the last estimate or reported value. We assume companies with shrinking free cash flow will slow their rate of shrinkage, and that companies with growing free cash flow will see their growth rate slow, over this period. We do this to reflect that growth tends to slow more in the early years than it does in later years.A DCF is all about the idea that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today, so we discount the value of these future cash flows to their estimated value in today's dollars:Story continues10-year free cash flow (FCF) estimate2024202520262027202820292030203120322033 Levered FCF ($, Millions) US$2.42bUS$3.02bUS$3.45bUS$3.68bUS$3.86bUS$4.02bUS$4.16bUS$4.29bUS$4.41bUS$4.52bGrowth Rate Estimate SourceAnalyst x14Analyst x7Analyst x3Analyst x3Est @ 4.89%Est @ 4.05%Est @ 3.47%Est @ 3.06%Est @ 2.78%Est @ 2.58% Present Value ($, Millions) Discounted @ 7.9% US$2.2kUS$2.6kUS$2.7kUS$2.7kUS$2.6kUS$2.5kUS$2.4kUS$2.3kUS$2.2kUS$2.1k("Est" = FCF growth rate estimated by Simply Wall St)Present Value of 10-year Cash Flow (PVCF) = US$25bAfter calculating the present value of future cash flows in the initial 10-year period, we need to calculate the Terminal Value, which accounts for all future cash flows beyond the first stage. For a number of reasons a very conservative growth rate is used that cannot exceed that of a country's GDP growth. In this case we have used the 5-year average of the 10-year government bond yield (2.1%) to estimate future growth. In the same way as with the 10-year 'growth' period, we discount future cash flows to today's value, using a cost of equity of 7.9%.Terminal Value (TV)= FCF2033 × (1 + g) ÷ (r – g) = US$4.5b× (1 + 2.1%) ÷ (7.9%– 2.1%) = US$79bPresent Value of Terminal Value (PVTV)= TV / (1 + r)10= US$79b÷ ( 1 + 7.9%)10= US$37bThe total value, or equity value, is then the sum of the present value of the future cash flows, which in this case is US$61b. The last step is to then divide the equity value by the number of shares outstanding. Relative to the current share price of US$171, the company appears around fair value at the time of writing. Remember though, that this is just an approximate valuation, and like any complex formula - garbage in, garbage out.dcfThe AssumptionsNow the most important inputs to a discounted cash flow are the discount rate, and of course, the actual cash flows. If you don't agree with these result, have a go at the calculation yourself and play with the assumptions. The DCF also does not consider the possible cyclicality of an industry, or a company's future capital requirements, so it does not give a full picture of a company's potential performance. Given that we are looking at Waste Management as potential shareholders, the cost of equity is used as the discount rate, rather than the cost of capital (or weighted average cost of capital, WACC) which accounts for debt. In this calculation we've used 7.9%, which is based on a levered beta of 0.981. Beta is a measure of a stock's volatility, compared to the market as a whole. We get our beta from the industry average beta of globally comparable companies, with an imposed limit between 0.8 and 2.0, which is a reasonable range for a stable business.SWOT Analysis for Waste ManagementStrengthEarnings growth over the past year exceeded the industry.Debt is well covered by earnings and cashflows.Dividends are covered by earnings and cash flows.WeaknessDividend is low compared to the top 25% of dividend payers in the Commercial Services market.OpportunityAnnual earnings are forecast to grow for the next 3 years.Good value based on P/E ratio compared to estimated Fair P/E ratio.ThreatAnnual earnings are forecast to grow slower than the American market.Moving On:Although the valuation of a company is important, it is only one of many factors that you need to assess for a company. DCF models are not the be-all and end-all of investment valuation. Instead the best use for a DCF model is to test certain assumptions and theories to see if they would lead to the company being undervalued or overvalued. If a company grows at a different rate, or if its cost of equity or risk free rate changes sharply, the output can look very different. (NYSE:WM) from its intrinsic value? Using the most recent financial data, we'll take a look at whether the stock is fairly priced by taking the forecast future cash flows of the company and discounting them back to today's value. We will take advantage of the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model for this purpose. It may sound complicated, but actually it is quite simple!We generally believe that a company's value is the present value of all of the cash it will generate in the future. However, a DCF is just one valuation metric among many, and it is not without flaws. For those who are keen learners of equity analysis, the Simply Wall St analysis model here may be something of interest to you. Check out our latest analysis for Waste Management The ModelWe are going to use a two-stage DCF model, which, as the name states, takes into account two stages of growth. The first stage is generally a higher growth period which levels off heading towards the terminal value, captured in the second 'steady growth' period. To start off with, we need to estimate the next ten years of cash flows. Where possible we use analyst estimates, but when these aren't available we extrapolate the previous free cash flow (FCF) from the last estimate or reported value. We assume companies with shrinking free cash flow will slow their rate of shrinkage, and that companies with growing free cash flow will see their growth rate slow, over this period. We do this to reflect that growth tends to slow more in the early years than it does in later years.A DCF is all about the idea that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today, so we discount the value of these future cash flows to their estimated value in today's dollars:Story continues10-year free cash flow (FCF) estimate2024202520262027202820292030203120322033 Levered FCF ($, Millions) US$2.42bUS$3.02bUS$3.45bUS$3.68bUS$3.86bUS$4.02bUS$4.16bUS$4.29bUS$4.41bUS$4.52bGrowth Rate Estimate SourceAnalyst x14Analyst x7Analyst x3Analyst x3Est @ 4.89%Est @ 4.05%Est @ 3.47%Est @ 3.06%Est @ 2.78%Est @ 2.58% Present Value ($, Millions) Discounted @ 7.9% US$2.2kUS$2.6kUS$2.7kUS$2.7kUS$2.6kUS$2.5kUS$2.4kUS$2.3kUS$2.2kUS$2.1k("Est" = FCF growth rate estimated by Simply Wall St)Present Value of 10-year Cash Flow (PVCF) = US$25bAfter calculating the present value of future cash flows in the initial 10-year period, we need to calculate the Terminal Value, which accounts for all future cash flows beyond the first stage. For a number of reasons a very conservative growth rate is used that cannot exceed that of a country's GDP growth. In this case we have used the 5-year average of the 10-year government bond yield (2.1%) to estimate future growth. In the same way as with the 10-year 'growth' period, we discount future cash flows to today's value, using a cost of equity of 7.9%.Terminal Value (TV)= FCF2033 × (1 + g) ÷ (r – g) = US$4.5b× (1 + 2.1%) ÷ (7.9%– 2.1%) = US$79bPresent Value of Terminal Value (PVTV)= TV / (1 + r)10= US$79b÷ ( 1 + 7.9%)10= US$37bThe total value, or equity value, is then the sum of the present value of the future cash flows, which in this case is US$61b. The last step is to then divide the equity value by the number of shares outstanding. Relative to the current share price of US$171, the company appears around fair value at the time of writing. Remember though, that this is just an approximate valuation, and like any complex formula - garbage in, garbage out.dcfThe AssumptionsNow the most important inputs to a discounted cash flow are the discount rate, and of course, the actual cash flows. If you don't agree with these result, have a go at the calculation yourself and play with the assumptions. The DCF also does not consider the possible cyclicality of an industry, or a company's future capital requirements, so it does not give a full picture of a company's potential performance. Given that we are looking at Waste Management as potential shareholders, the cost of equity is used as the discount rate, rather than the cost of capital (or weighted average cost of capital, WACC) which accounts for debt. In this calculation we've used 7.9%, which is based on a levered beta of 0.981. Beta is a measure of a stock's volatility, compared to the market as a whole. We get our beta from the industry average beta of globally comparable companies, with an imposed limit between 0.8 and 2.0, which is a reasonable range for a stable business.SWOT Analysis for Waste ManagementStrengthEarnings growth over the past year exceeded the industry.Debt is well covered by earnings and cashflows.Dividends are covered by earnings and cash flows.WeaknessDividend is low compared to the top 25% of dividend payers in the Commercial Services market.OpportunityAnnual earnings are forecast to grow for the next 3 years.Good value based on P/E ratio compared to estimated Fair P/E ratio.ThreatAnnual earnings are forecast to grow slower than the American market.Moving On:Although the valuation of a company is important, it is only one of many factors that you need to assess for a company. DCF models are not the be-all and end-all of investment valuation. Instead the best use for a DCF model is to test certain assumptions and theories to see if they would lead to the company being undervalued or overvalued. If a company grows at a different rate, or if its cost of equity or risk free rate changes sharply, the output can look very different. column4: A Look At The Fair Value Of Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM)
column10: [Key InsightsThe projected fair value for Waste Management is US$151 based on 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to EquityWith US$171 share price, Waste Management appears to be trading close to its estimated fair value Analyst price target for WM is US$175, which is 16% above our fair value estimateHow far off is Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM) from its intrinsic value? Using the most recent financial data, we'll take a look at whether the stock is fairly priced by taking the forecast future cash flows of the company and discounting them back to today's value. We will take advantage of the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model for this purpose. It may sound complicated, but actually it is quite simple!We generally believe that a company's value is the present value of all of the cash it will generate in the future. However, a DCF is just one valuation metric among many, and it is not without flaws. For those who are keen learners of equity analysis, the Simply Wall St analysis model here may be something of interest to you. Check out our latest analysis for Waste Management The ModelWe are going to use a two-stage DCF model, which, as the name states, takes into account two stages of growth. The first stage is generally a higher growth period which levels off heading towards the terminal value, captured in the second 'steady growth' period. To start off with, we need to estimate the next ten years of cash flows. Where possible we use analyst estimates, but when these aren't available we extrapolate the previous free cash flow (FCF) from the last estimate or reported value. We assume companies with shrinking free cash flow will slow their rate of shrinkage, and that companies with growing free cash flow will see their growth rate slow, over this period. We do this to reflect that growth tends to slow more in the early years than it does in later years.A DCF is all about the idea that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today, so we discount the value of these future cash flows to their estimated value in today's dollars:Story continues10-year free cash flow (FCF) estimate2024202520262027202820292030203120322033 Levered FCF ($, Millions) US$2.42bUS$3.02bUS$3.45bUS$3.68bUS$3.86bUS$4.02bUS$4.16bUS$4.29bUS$4.41bUS$4.52bGrowth Rate Estimate SourceAnalyst x14Analyst x7Analyst x3Analyst x3Est @ 4.89%Est @ 4.05%Est @ 3.47%Est @ 3.06%Est @ 2.78%Est @ 2.58% Present Value ($, Millions) Discounted @ 7.9% US$2.2kUS$2.6kUS$2.7kUS$2.7kUS$2.6kUS$2.5kUS$2.4kUS$2.3kUS$2.2kUS$2.1k("Est" = FCF growth rate estimated by Simply Wall St)Present Value of 10-year Cash Flow (PVCF) = US$25bAfter calculating the present value of future cash flows in the initial 10-year period, we need to calculate the Terminal Value, which accounts for all future cash flows beyond the first stage. For a number of reasons a very conservative growth rate is used that cannot exceed that of a country's GDP growth. In this case we have used the 5-year average of the 10-year government bond yield (2.1%) to estimate future growth. In the same way as with the 10-year 'growth' period, we discount future cash flows to today's value, using a cost of equity of 7.9%.Terminal Value (TV)= FCF2033 × (1 + g) ÷ (r – g) = US$4.5b× (1 + 2.1%) ÷ (7.9%– 2.1%) = US$79bPresent Value of Terminal Value (PVTV)= TV / (1 + r)10= US$79b÷ ( 1 + 7.9%)10= US$37bThe total value, or equity value, is then the sum of the present value of the future cash flows, which in this case is US$61b. The last step is to then divide the equity value by the number of shares outstanding. Relative to the current share price of US$171, the company appears around fair value at the time of writing. Remember though, that this is just an approximate valuation, and like any complex formula - garbage in, garbage out.dcfThe AssumptionsNow the most important inputs to a discounted cash flow are the discount rate, and of course, the actual cash flows. If you don't agree with these result, have a go at the calculation yourself and play with the assumptions. The DCF also does not consider the possible cyclicality of an industry, or a company's future capital requirements, so it does not give a full picture of a company's potential performance. Given that we are looking at Waste Management as potential shareholders, the cost of equity is used as the discount rate, rather than the cost of capital (or weighted average cost of capital, WACC) which accounts for debt. In this calculation we've used 7.9%, which is based on a levered beta of 0.981. Beta is a measure of a stock's volatility, compared to the market as a whole. We get our beta from the industry average beta of globally comparable companies, with an imposed limit between 0.8 and 2.0, which is a reasonable range for a stable business.SWOT Analysis for Waste ManagementStrengthEarnings growth over the past year exceeded the industry.Debt is well covered by earnings and cashflows.Dividends are covered by earnings and cash flows.WeaknessDividend is low compared to the top 25% of dividend payers in the Commercial Services market.OpportunityAnnual earnings are forecast to grow for the next 3 years.Good value based on P/E ratio compared to estimated Fair P/E ratio.ThreatAnnual earnings are forecast to grow slower than the American market.Moving On:Although the valuation of a company is important, it is only one of many factors that you need to assess for a company. DCF models are not the be-all and end-all of investment valuation. Instead the best use for a DCF model is to test certain assumptions and theories to see if they would lead to the company being undervalued or overvalued. If a company grows at a different rate, or if its cost of equity or risk free rate changes sharply, the output can look very different. column4: A Look At The Fair Value Of Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM)
column10: [Key InsightsThe projected fair value for Waste Management is US$151 based on 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to EquityWith US$171 share price, Waste Management appears to be trading close to its estimated fair value Analyst price target for WM is US$175, which is 16% above our fair value estimateHow far off is Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM) from its intrinsic value? Using the most recent financial data, we'll take a look at whether the stock is fairly priced by taking the forecast future cash flows of the company and discounting them back to today's value. We will take advantage of the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model for this purpose. It may sound complicated, but actually it is quite simple!We generally believe that a company's value is the present value of all of the cash it will generate in the future. However, a DCF is just one valuation metric among many, and it is not without flaws. For those who are keen learners of equity analysis, the Simply Wall St analysis model here may be something of interest to you. Check out our latest analysis for Waste Management The ModelWe are going to use a two-stage DCF model, which, as the name states, takes into account two stages of growth. The first stage is generally a higher growth period which levels off heading towards the terminal value, captured in the second 'steady growth' period. To start off with, we need to estimate the next ten years of cash flows. Where possible we use analyst estimates, but when these aren't available we extrapolate the previous free cash flow (FCF) from the last estimate or reported value. We assume companies with shrinking free cash flow will slow their rate of shrinkage, and that companies with growing free cash flow will see their growth rate slow, over this period. We do this to reflect that growth tends to slow more in the early years than it does in later years.A DCF is all about the idea that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today, so we discount the value of these future cash flows to their estimated value in today's dollars:Story continues10-year free cash flow (FCF) estimate2024202520262027202820292030203120322033 Levered FCF ($, Millions) US$2.42bUS$3.02bUS$3.45bUS$3.68bUS$3.86bUS$4.02bUS$4.16bUS$4.29bUS$4.41bUS$4.52bGrowth Rate Estimate SourceAnalyst x14Analyst x7Analyst x3Analyst x3Est @ 4.89%Est @ 4.05%Est @ 3.47%Est @ 3.06%Est @ 2.78%Est @ 2.58% Present Value ($, Millions) Discounted @ 7.9% US$2.2kUS$2.6kUS$2.7kUS$2.7kUS$2.6kUS$2.5kUS$2.4kUS$2.3kUS$2.2kUS$2.1k("Est" = FCF growth rate estimated by Simply Wall St)Present Value of 10-year Cash Flow (PVCF) = US$25bAfter calculating the present value of future cash flows in the initial 10-year period, we need to calculate the Terminal Value, which accounts for all future cash flows beyond the first stage. For a number of reasons a very conservative growth rate is used that cannot exceed that of a country's GDP growth. In this case we have used the 5-year average of the 10-year government bond yield (2.1%) to estimate future growth. In the same way as with the 10-year 'growth' period, we discount future cash flows to today's value, using a cost of equity of 7.9%.Terminal Value (TV)= FCF2033 × (1 + g) ÷ (r – g) = US$4.5b× (1 + 2.1%) ÷ (7.9%– 2.1%) = US$79bPresent Value of Terminal Value (PVTV)= TV / (1 + r)10= US$79b÷ ( 1 + 7.9%)10= US$37bThe total value, or equity value, is then the sum of the present value of the future cash flows, which in this case is US$61b. The last step is to then divide the equity value by the number of shares outstanding. Relative to the current share price of US$171, the company appears around fair value at the time of writing. Remember though, that this is just an approximate valuation, and like any complex formula - garbage in, garbage out.dcfThe AssumptionsNow the most important inputs to a discounted cash flow are the discount rate, and of course, the actual cash flows. If you don't agree with these result, have a go at the calculation yourself and play with the assumptions. The DCF also does not consider the possible cyclicality of an industry, or a company's future capital requirements, so it does not give a full picture of a company's potential performance. Given that we are looking at Waste Management as potential shareholders, the cost of equity is used as the discount rate, rather than the cost of capital (or weighted average cost of capital, WACC) which accounts for debt. In this calculation we've used 7.9%, which is based on a levered beta of 0.981. Beta is a measure of a stock's volatility, compared to the market as a whole. We get our beta from the industry average beta of globally comparable companies, with an imposed limit between 0.8 and 2.0, which is a reasonable range for a stable business.SWOT Analysis for Waste ManagementStrengthEarnings growth over the past year exceeded the industry.Debt is well covered by earnings and cashflows.Dividends are covered by earnings and cash flows.WeaknessDividend is low compared to the top 25% of dividend payers in the Commercial Services market.OpportunityAnnual earnings are forecast to grow for the next 3 years.Good value based on P/E ratio compared to estimated Fair P/E ratio.ThreatAnnual earnings are forecast to grow slower than the American market.Moving On:Although the valuation of a company is important, it is only one of many factors that you need to assess for a company. DCF models are not the be-all and end-all of investment valuation. Instead the best use for a DCF model is to test certain assumptions and theories to see if they would lead to the company being undervalued or overvalued. If a company grows at a different rate, or if its cost of equity or risk free rate changes sharply, the output can look very different. The first stage is generally a higher growth period which levels off heading towards the terminal value, captured in the second 'steady growth' period. To start off with, we need to estimate the next ten years of cash flows. Where possible we use analyst estimates, but when these aren't available we extrapolate the previous free cash flow (FCF) from the last estimate or reported value. We assume companies with shrinking free cash flow will slow their rate of shrinkage, and that companies with growing free cash flow will see their growth rate slow, over this period. We do this to reflect that growth tends to slow more in the early years than it does in later years.A DCF is all about the idea that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today, so we discount the value of these future cash flows to their estimated value in today's dollars:Story continues10-year free cash flow (FCF) estimate2024202520262027202820292030203120322033 Levered FCF ($, Millions) US$2.42bUS$3.02bUS$3.45bUS$3.68bUS$3.86bUS$4.02bUS$4.16bUS$4.29bUS$4.41bUS$4.52bGrowth Rate Estimate SourceAnalyst x14Analyst x7Analyst x3Analyst x3Est @ 4.89%Est @ 4.05%Est @ 3.47%Est @ 3.06%Est @ 2.78%Est @ 2.58% Present Value ($, Millions) Discounted @ 7.9% US$2.2kUS$2.6kUS$2.7kUS$2.7kUS$2.6kUS$2.5kUS$2.4kUS$2.3kUS$2.2kUS$2.1k("Est" = FCF growth rate estimated by Simply Wall St)Present Value of 10-year Cash Flow (PVCF) = US$25bAfter calculating the present value of future cash flows in the initial 10-year period, we need to calculate the Terminal Value, which accounts for all future cash flows beyond the first stage. For a number of reasons a very conservative growth rate is used that cannot exceed that of a country's GDP growth. In this case we have used the 5-year average of the 10-year government bond yield (2.1%) to estimate future growth. In the same way as with the 10-year 'growth' period, we discount future cash flows to today's value, using a cost of equity of 7.9%.Terminal Value (TV)= FCF2033 × (1 + g) ÷ (r – g) = US$4.5b× (1 + 2.1%) ÷ (7.9%– 2.1%) = US$79bPresent Value of Terminal Value (PVTV)= TV / (1 + r)10= US$79b÷ ( 1 + 7.9%)10= US$37bThe total value, or equity value, is then the sum of the present value of the future cash flows, which in this case is US$61b. The last step is to then divide the equity value by the number of shares outstanding. Relative to the current share price of US$171, the company appears around fair value at the time of writing. Remember though, that this is just an approximate valuation, and like any complex formula - garbage in, garbage out.dcfThe AssumptionsNow the most important inputs to a discounted cash flow are the discount rate, and of course, the actual cash flows. If you don't agree with these result, have a go at the calculation yourself and play with the assumptions. The DCF also does not consider the possible cyclicality of an industry, or a company's future capital requirements, so it does not give a full picture of a company's potential performance. Given that we are looking at Waste Management as potential shareholders, the cost of equity is used as the discount rate, rather than the cost of capital (or weighted average cost of capital, WACC) which accounts for debt. In this calculation we've used 7.9%, which is based on a levered beta of 0.981. Beta is a measure of a stock's volatility, compared to the market as a whole. We get our beta from the industry average beta of globally comparable companies, with an imposed limit between 0.8 and 2.0, which is a reasonable range for a stable business.SWOT Analysis for Waste ManagementStrengthEarnings growth over the past year exceeded the industry.Debt is well covered by earnings and cashflows.Dividends are covered by earnings and cash flows.WeaknessDividend is low compared to the top 25% of dividend payers in the Commercial Services market.OpportunityAnnual earnings are forecast to grow for the next 3 years.Good value based on P/E ratio compared to estimated Fair P/E ratio.ThreatAnnual earnings are forecast to grow slower than the American market.Moving On:Although the valuation of a company is important, it is only one of many factors that you need to assess for a company. DCF models are not the be-all and end-all of investment valuation. Instead the best use for a DCF model is to test certain assumptions and theories to see if they would lead to the company being undervalued or overvalued. If a company grows at a different rate, or if its cost of equity or risk free rate changes sharply, the output can look very different. column4: 7 Stocks to Buy Now if You Still Think a Recession Is Ahead
column10: [Preparing for a recession at this juncture seems a ridiculous concept at this juncture. As CNBC pointed out late last week, the Federal Reserve’s key inflation measure showed that prices increased by just 0.3% in May, favorably below expectations. Put another way, disinflation is occurring which means that recession-proof stocks are only for worrywarts, right?Well, maybe not. While the inflation data is encouraging, it’s also worth pointing out that the U.S. Supreme Court struck down President Biden’s plan to forgive student debt. That will likely weigh on discretionary retail sectors as affected individuals face a harsh reality check. Thus, it’s still a good idea to at least consider safe stocks in a recession.Also, credit card debt hit a record high, implying that the Covid-19 pandemic failed to teach financial prudence. Should circumstances go awry, many if not most households lack the wherewithal to navigate effectively. Therefore, the below recession stocks to buy remain relevant despite the latest headline numbers.InvestorPlace - Stock Market News, Stock Advice & Trading TipsRecession-Proof Stocks: Waste Management (WM)man's hand holding wads of cash. stocks to buy. Therefore, Waste Management enjoys an entrenched natural monopoly.On the financial side, about the only major source of hesitation toward WM as a vehicle for investing during a recession is the valuation prospect. Trading at a forward multiple of 28.64, acquiring WM commands a hefty premium since the underlying sector’s median forward price-earnings ratio is only 19.23 times.Nevertheless, what I appreciate about WM is its strong three-year revenue growth rate (per-share basis) of 9.5%. As a result, it’s one of the safe stocks in recession because everybody generates trash, downturn or not.Story continuesRecession-Proof Stocks: Colgate-Palmolive (CL)An image of a street sign post with directions labeled "Buy", "Hold", and "Sell"Source: PX Media / ShutterstockAnother almost self-explanatory case for recession-proof stocks to buy, Colgate-Palmolive (NYSE:CL) is a major player in the personal care segment. Fundamentally, what I appreciate about Colgate is its namesake products for toothcare. Irrespective of whether a recession materializes or not, people will brush their teeth. It’s also one of the easiest processes involved regarding preventative care.Regarding the financial aspect, Colgate again suffers a similar dilemma to Waste Management. Basically, as one of the more obvious ideas for recession stocks to buy, several folks have already piled into CL. Right now, shares trade at a forward multiple of 24.62. In contrast, the underlying sector median stat is 16.63 times. Thus, we’re talking about a sizeable premium.On the other hand, Colgate also benefits from consistent profitability, making it an appropriate idea if you’re preparing for a recession. Put another way, business predictability should command its own premium during a down cycle.Recession-Proof Stocks: Kroger (KR)Man holding stacks of money. Unknown Millionaire-Maker StocksSource: Epic Cure / ShutterstockAgain, Kroger (NYSE:KR) presents an intuitive canvas for recession-proof stocks to buy. As a major player in the supermarket segment, Kroger stands to benefit from the trade-down effect. This concept involves consumers trading down their common purchases for cheaper alternatives (rather than going cold turkey). By logical deduction, Kroger represents a trade-down for consumers who previously went out to restaurants or ordered food deliveries.Financially, Kroger presents a very intriguing argument for investing during a recession. Sure, the company only features a trailing-year net margin of 1.71%, which is slightly worse than the sector median of 1.82%. At the same time, Kroger carries a three-year revenue growth rate of 10.3%, outpacing nearly 70% of sector rivals.Most enticingly, the market prices KR at a forward multiple of 10.44. As a discount to projected earnings, Kroger ranks better than 83.08% of enterprises in the defensive retail space. Also, it trades at 0.23 times trailing sales, favorably below 69.9% of its peers. Thus, it’s one of the safe stocks in recession.Five Below (FIVE)A person draws a stock chart on a chalkboard.Source: Zurijeta / Shutterstock.comWhile I’m a big fan of discount dollar stores as a frontline strategy for recession-proof stocks, they can also be problematic. Let’s face reality: dollar stores tend to be grimy affairs that might not attract customers during non-recession years. Fortunately, Five Below (NASDAQ:FIVE) fills a nice niche in the discount retail space.Offering products priced mostly at five bucks but also select products that run to $25, Five Below delivers a bargain and a touch of class. Therefore, it should be relevant irrespective of whatever’s happening with the economy.On a financial basis, Five Below benefits from a strong three-year revenue growth rate of 18.8%, above 80.44% of its peers. Also, its EBITDA growth rate clocks in at 18.6% during the same period. Additionally, concerned investors will likely appreciate Five Below’s consistent profitability. To be fair, FIVE carries a rich premium to both earnings and sales. Still, if circumstances go awry, Five Below will likely swing much higher from here.Sempra Energy (SRE)hands at desk near laptop computer, with one hand holding a pile of hundred dollar bills. Bank stocksSource: shutterstock.com/CC7Speaking of natural monopolies, Sempra Energy (NYSE:SRE) commands one of the most lucrative. First, Sempra of course represents a major player in the public utility space. No matter what happens with the market or the economy, you must still pay your bills. And not that I know from personal experience but these folks hunt you down if you forget to pay.Second, Sempra serves large portions of the Southern California market, which isn’t surprising given its San Diego headquarters. As you know, California – despite its criticisms – is the economic engine of this nation. By logical deduction, Sempra serves the residents of this economic engine. Stated differently, it’s going to get its bills paid, downturn or no downturn.Therefore, SRE easily ranks among the recession-proof stocks to buy. In all fairness, Sempra’s financials leave much to be desired on paper. However, the biggest takeaway is that it’s consistently profitable, which isn’t a shocker. Thus, put shares on your radar if you’re investing during a recession.Archer Daniels Midland (ADM)tree growing on coin of stacking with green bokeh background; growth stocksSource: Freedom365day / Shutterstock.comA food processing and commodities trading company, Archer Daniels Midland (NYSE:ADM) offers a complete portfolio of ingredients and solutions to meet any taste and a commitment to sustainability, according to its corporate profile. If you want to know, it’s that humans obviously have to eat.What’s really interesting about ADM centers on its value proposition. A cursory glance at its business model will reveal that ADM presents an obvious case for safe stocks in recession. You’d think people would be all over Archer Daniels. Instead, the market prices shares at a forward multiple of only 11.34. As a discount to projected earnings, the company ranks better than 76.52% of its peers.In addition, Archer features a three-year revenue growth rate of 16.4%, beating out 76.67% of entities in the consumer packaged goods space. Also, its EBITDA growth rate during the same frame clocks in at an impressive 30.8%. Thus, it’s one of the recession stocks to buy.Essential Utilities (WTRG)Stocks to buy: smartphone with the words "buy" and "sell" displayed on the screen. The user's finger is about to press buy. Since the January opener, WTRG slipped more than 17%. Even with that magnitude of red ink, shares appear overvalued against both trailing and forward earnings.Still, Essential carries one of the most important attributes when it comes to investing during a recession: consistent profitability. Also, it packs a stout top line with a three-year revenue growth rate of 28.3%, beating out 91.87% of its peers. On a final note, analysts peg WTRG as a moderate buy with a price target of $50.50. Increasing dividends mean shareholders receive larger cash payments over time. Moreover, companies that raise their payouts regularly have outperformed the market historically. According to a report by T. Rowe Price, the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrat Index, which tracks the performance of companies with 25 consecutive years of dividend increases, has outperformed the S&P 500 by over 75% since 1989. column10: [Key InsightsThe projected fair value for Waste Management is US$151 based on 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to EquityWith US$171 share price, Waste Management appears to be trading close to its estimated fair value Analyst price target for WM is US$175, which is 16% above our fair value estimateHow far off is Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM) from its intrinsic value? Using the most recent financial data, we'll take a look at whether the stock is fairly priced by taking the forecast future cash flows of the company and discounting them back to today's value. We will take advantage of the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model for this purpose. It may sound complicated, but actually it is quite simple!We generally believe that a company's value is the present value of all of the cash it will generate in the future. However, a DCF is just one valuation metric among many, and it is not without flaws. For those who are keen learners of equity analysis, the Simply Wall St analysis model here may be something of interest to you. Check out our latest analysis for Waste Management The ModelWe are going to use a two-stage DCF model, which, as the name states, takes into account two stages of growth. The first stage is generally a higher growth period which levels off heading towards the terminal value, captured in the second 'steady growth' period. To start off with, we need to estimate the next ten years of cash flows. Where possible we use analyst estimates, but when these aren't available we extrapolate the previous free cash flow (FCF) from the last estimate or reported value. We assume companies with shrinking free cash flow will slow their rate of shrinkage, and that companies with growing free cash flow will see their growth rate slow, over this period. We do this to reflect that growth tends to slow more in the early years than it does in later years.A DCF is all about the idea that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today, so we discount the value of these future cash flows to their estimated value in today's dollars:Story continues10-year free cash flow (FCF) estimate2024202520262027202820292030203120322033 Levered FCF ($, Millions) US$2.42bUS$3.02bUS$3.45bUS$3.68bUS$3.86bUS$4.02bUS$4.16bUS$4.29bUS$4.41bUS$4.52bGrowth Rate Estimate SourceAnalyst x14Analyst x7Analyst x3Analyst x3Est @ 4.89%Est @ 4.05%Est @ 3.47%Est @ 3.06%Est @ 2.78%Est @ 2.58% Present Value ($, Millions) Discounted @ 7.9% US$2.2kUS$2.6kUS$2.7kUS$2.7kUS$2.6kUS$2.5kUS$2.4kUS$2.3kUS$2.2kUS$2.1k("Est" = FCF growth rate estimated by Simply Wall St)Present Value of 10-year Cash Flow (PVCF) = US$25bAfter calculating the present value of future cash flows in the initial 10-year period, we need to calculate the Terminal Value, which accounts for all future cash flows beyond the first stage. For a number of reasons a very conservative growth rate is used that cannot exceed that of a country's GDP growth. In this case we have used the 5-year average of the 10-year government bond yield (2.1%) to estimate future growth. In the same way as with the 10-year 'growth' period, we discount future cash flows to today's value, using a cost of equity of 7.9%.Terminal Value (TV)= FCF2033 × (1 + g) ÷ (r – g) = US$4.5b× (1 + 2.1%) ÷ (7.9%– 2.1%) = US$79bPresent Value of Terminal Value (PVTV)= TV / (1 + r)10= US$79b÷ ( 1 + 7.9%)10= US$37bThe total value, or equity value, is then the sum of the present value of the future cash flows, which in this case is US$61b. The last step is to then divide the equity value by the number of shares outstanding. Relative to the current share price of US$171, the company appears around fair value at the time of writing. Remember though, that this is just an approximate valuation, and like any complex formula - garbage in, garbage out.dcfThe AssumptionsNow the most important inputs to a discounted cash flow are the discount rate, and of course, the actual cash flows. If you don't agree with these result, have a go at the calculation yourself and play with the assumptions. The DCF also does not consider the possible cyclicality of an industry, or a company's future capital requirements, so it does not give a full picture of a company's potential performance. Given that we are looking at Waste Management as potential shareholders, the cost of equity is used as the discount rate, rather than the cost of capital (or weighted average cost of capital, WACC) which accounts for debt. In this calculation we've used 7.9%, which is based on a levered beta of 0.981. Beta is a measure of a stock's volatility, compared to the market as a whole. We get our beta from the industry average beta of globally comparable companies, with an imposed limit between 0.8 and 2.0, which is a reasonable range for a stable business.SWOT Analysis for Waste ManagementStrengthEarnings growth over the past year exceeded the industry.Debt is well covered by earnings and cashflows.Dividends are covered by earnings and cash flows.WeaknessDividend is low compared to the top 25% of dividend payers in the Commercial Services market.OpportunityAnnual earnings are forecast to grow for the next 3 years.Good value based on P/E ratio compared to estimated Fair P/E ratio.ThreatAnnual earnings are forecast to grow slower than the American market.Moving On:Although the valuation of a company is important, it is only one of many factors that you need to assess for a company. DCF models are not the be-all and end-all of investment valuation. Instead the best use for a DCF model is to test certain assumptions and theories to see if they would lead to the company being undervalued or overvalued. If a company grows at a different rate, or if its cost of equity or risk free rate changes sharply, the output can look very different. Using the most recent financial data, we'll take a look at whether the stock is fairly priced by taking the forecast future cash flows of the company and discounting them back to today's value. We will take advantage of the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model for this purpose. It may sound complicated, but actually it is quite simple!We generally believe that a company's value is the present value of all of the cash it will generate in the future. However, a DCF is just one valuation metric among many, and it is not without flaws. For those who are keen learners of equity analysis, the Simply Wall St analysis model here may be something of interest to you. Check out our latest analysis for Waste Management The ModelWe are going to use a two-stage DCF model, which, as the name states, takes into account two stages of growth. The first stage is generally a higher growth period which levels off heading towards the terminal value, captured in the second 'steady growth' period. To start off with, we need to estimate the next ten years of cash flows. Where possible we use analyst estimates, but when these aren't available we extrapolate the previous free cash flow (FCF) from the last estimate or reported value. We assume companies with shrinking free cash flow will slow their rate of shrinkage, and that companies with growing free cash flow will see their growth rate slow, over this period. We do this to reflect that growth tends to slow more in the early years than it does in later years.A DCF is all about the idea that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today, so we discount the value of these future cash flows to their estimated value in today's dollars:Story continues10-year free cash flow (FCF) estimate2024202520262027202820292030203120322033 Levered FCF ($, Millions) US$2.42bUS$3.02bUS$3.45bUS$3.68bUS$3.86bUS$4.02bUS$4.16bUS$4.29bUS$4.41bUS$4.52bGrowth Rate Estimate SourceAnalyst x14Analyst x7Analyst x3Analyst x3Est @ 4.89%Est @ 4.05%Est @ 3.47%Est @ 3.06%Est @ 2.78%Est @ 2.58% Present Value ($, Millions) Discounted @ 7.9% US$2.2kUS$2.6kUS$2.7kUS$2.7kUS$2.6kUS$2.5kUS$2.4kUS$2.3kUS$2.2kUS$2.1k("Est" = FCF growth rate estimated by Simply Wall St)Present Value of 10-year Cash Flow (PVCF) = US$25bAfter calculating the present value of future cash flows in the initial 10-year period, we need to calculate the Terminal Value, which accounts for all future cash flows beyond the first stage. For a number of reasons a very conservative growth rate is used that cannot exceed that of a country's GDP growth. In this case we have used the 5-year average of the 10-year government bond yield (2.1%) to estimate future growth. In the same way as with the 10-year 'growth' period, we discount future cash flows to today's value, using a cost of equity of 7.9%.Terminal Value (TV)= FCF2033 × (1 + g) ÷ (r – g) = US$4.5b× (1 + 2.1%) ÷ (7.9%– 2.1%) = US$79bPresent Value of Terminal Value (PVTV)= TV / (1 + r)10= US$79b÷ ( 1 + 7.9%)10= US$37bThe total value, or equity value, is then the sum of the present value of the future cash flows, which in this case is US$61b. The last step is to then divide the equity value by the number of shares outstanding. Relative to the current share price of US$171, the company appears around fair value at the time of writing. Remember though, that this is just an approximate valuation, and like any complex formula - garbage in, garbage out.dcfThe AssumptionsNow the most important inputs to a discounted cash flow are the discount rate, and of course, the actual cash flows. If you don't agree with these result, have a go at the calculation yourself and play with the assumptions. The DCF also does not consider the possible cyclicality of an industry, or a company's future capital requirements, so it does not give a full picture of a company's potential performance. Given that we are looking at Waste Management as potential shareholders, the cost of equity is used as the discount rate, rather than the cost of capital (or weighted average cost of capital, WACC) which accounts for debt. In this calculation we've used 7.9%, which is based on a levered beta of 0.981. Beta is a measure of a stock's volatility, compared to the market as a whole. We get our beta from the industry average beta of globally comparable companies, with an imposed limit between 0.8 and 2.0, which is a reasonable range for a stable business.SWOT Analysis for Waste ManagementStrengthEarnings growth over the past year exceeded the industry.Debt is well covered by earnings and cashflows.Dividends are covered by earnings and cash flows.WeaknessDividend is low compared to the top 25% of dividend payers in the Commercial Services market.OpportunityAnnual earnings are forecast to grow for the next 3 years.Good value based on P/E ratio compared to estimated Fair P/E ratio.ThreatAnnual earnings are forecast to grow slower than the American market.Moving On:Although the valuation of a company is important, it is only one of many factors that you need to assess for a company. DCF models are not the be-all and end-all of investment valuation. Instead the best use for a DCF model is to test certain assumptions and theories to see if they would lead to the company being undervalued or overvalued. If a company grows at a different rate, or if its cost of equity or risk free rate changes sharply, the output can look very different. column4: 7 Stocks to Buy Now if You Still Think a Recession Is Ahead
column10: [Preparing for a recession at this juncture seems a ridiculous concept at this juncture. By logical deduction, Kroger represents a trade-down for consumers who previously went out to restaurants or ordered food deliveries.Financially, Kroger presents a very intriguing argument for investing during a recession. Thus, it’s one of the safe stocks in recession.Five Below (FIVE)A person draws a stock chart on a chalkboard.Source: Zurijeta / Shutterstock.comWhile I’m a big fan of discount dollar stores as a frontline strategy for recession-proof stocks, they can also be problematic. To calculate this metric for Waste Management, this is the formula:Return on Capital Employed = Earnings Before Interest and Tax (EBIT) ÷ (Total Assets - Current Liabilities)0.13 = US$3.5b ÷ (US$31b - US$3.9b) (Based on the trailing twelve months to March 2023).Therefore, Waste Management has an ROCE of 13%. column4: A Look At The Fair Value Of Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM)
column10: [Key InsightsThe projected fair value for Waste Management is US$151 based on 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to EquityWith US$171 share price, Waste Management appears to be trading close to its estimated fair value Analyst price target for WM is US$175, which is 16% above our fair value estimateHow far off is Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM) from its intrinsic value? Using the most recent financial data, we'll take a look at whether the stock is fairly priced by taking the forecast future cash flows of the company and discounting them back to today's value. We will take advantage of the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model for this purpose. It may sound complicated, but actually it is quite simple!We generally believe that a company's value is the present value of all of the cash it will generate in the future. However, a DCF is just one valuation metric among many, and it is not without flaws. For those who are keen learners of equity analysis, the Simply Wall St analysis model here may be something of interest to you. Check out our latest analysis for Waste Management The ModelWe are going to use a two-stage DCF model, which, as the name states, takes into account two stages of growth. The first stage is generally a higher growth period which levels off heading towards the terminal value, captured in the second 'steady growth' period. To start off with, we need to estimate the next ten years of cash flows. Where possible we use analyst estimates, but when these aren't available we extrapolate the previous free cash flow (FCF) from the last estimate or reported value. We assume companies with shrinking free cash flow will slow their rate of shrinkage, and that companies with growing free cash flow will see their growth rate slow, over this period. We do this to reflect that growth tends to slow more in the early years than it does in later years.A DCF is all about the idea that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today, so we discount the value of these future cash flows to their estimated value in today's dollars:Story continues10-year free cash flow (FCF) estimate2024202520262027202820292030203120322033 Levered FCF ($, Millions) US$2.42bUS$3.02bUS$3.45bUS$3.68bUS$3.86bUS$4.02bUS$4.16bUS$4.29bUS$4.41bUS$4.52bGrowth Rate Estimate SourceAnalyst x14Analyst x7Analyst x3Analyst x3Est @ 4.89%Est @ 4.05%Est @ 3.47%Est @ 3.06%Est @ 2.78%Est @ 2.58% Present Value ($, Millions) Discounted @ 7.9% US$2.2kUS$2.6kUS$2.7kUS$2.7kUS$2.6kUS$2.5kUS$2.4kUS$2.3kUS$2.2kUS$2.1k("Est" = FCF growth rate estimated by Simply Wall St)Present Value of 10-year Cash Flow (PVCF) = US$25bAfter calculating the present value of future cash flows in the initial 10-year period, we need to calculate the Terminal Value, which accounts for all future cash flows beyond the first stage. For a number of reasons a very conservative growth rate is used that cannot exceed that of a country's GDP growth. In this case we have used the 5-year average of the 10-year government bond yield (2.1%) to estimate future growth. In the same way as with the 10-year 'growth' period, we discount future cash flows to today's value, using a cost of equity of 7.9%.Terminal Value (TV)= FCF2033 × (1 + g) ÷ (r – g) = US$4.5b× (1 + 2.1%) ÷ (7.9%– 2.1%) = US$79bPresent Value of Terminal Value (PVTV)= TV / (1 + r)10= US$79b÷ ( 1 + 7.9%)10= US$37bThe total value, or equity value, is then the sum of the present value of the future cash flows, which in this case is US$61b. The last step is to then divide the equity value by the number of shares outstanding. Relative to the current share price of US$171, the company appears around fair value at the time of writing. Remember though, that this is just an approximate valuation, and like any complex formula - garbage in, garbage out.dcfThe AssumptionsNow the most important inputs to a discounted cash flow are the discount rate, and of course, the actual cash flows. If you don't agree with these result, have a go at the calculation yourself and play with the assumptions. The DCF also does not consider the possible cyclicality of an industry, or a company's future capital requirements, so it does not give a full picture of a company's potential performance. Given that we are looking at Waste Management as potential shareholders, the cost of equity is used as the discount rate, rather than the cost of capital (or weighted average cost of capital, WACC) which accounts for debt. In this calculation we've used 7.9%, which is based on a levered beta of 0.981. Beta is a measure of a stock's volatility, compared to the market as a whole. We get our beta from the industry average beta of globally comparable companies, with an imposed limit between 0.8 and 2.0, which is a reasonable range for a stable business.SWOT Analysis for Waste ManagementStrengthEarnings growth over the past year exceeded the industry.Debt is well covered by earnings and cashflows.Dividends are covered by earnings and cash flows.WeaknessDividend is low compared to the top 25% of dividend payers in the Commercial Services market.OpportunityAnnual earnings are forecast to grow for the next 3 years.Good value based on P/E ratio compared to estimated Fair P/E ratio.ThreatAnnual earnings are forecast to grow slower than the American market.Moving On:Although the valuation of a company is important, it is only one of many factors that you need to assess for a company. DCF models are not the be-all and end-all of investment valuation. Instead the best use for a DCF model is to test certain assumptions and theories to see if they would lead to the company being undervalued or overvalued. If a company grows at a different rate, or if its cost of equity or risk free rate changes sharply, the output can look very different. This implies the analysts working for those institutions have looked at the stock and they like it. But just like anyone else, they could be wrong. When multiple institutions own a stock, there's always a risk that they are in a 'crowded trade'. When such a trade goes wrong, multiple parties may compete to sell stock fast. column4: 25 Cleanest Countries In the World In 2023
column10: [This article will look at the 25 cleanest countries in the world that are performing well on multiple environmental indicators like climate change mitigation, waste management, and air quality. We'll also discuss the continuously deteriorating air and environmental quality. If you want to skip the details, read 10 Cleanest Countries In The World In 2023. Grading the 25 cleanest countries in the world in 2023 is a subjective topic that requires a deep dive into their environment-related efforts. For instance, the Environmental Performance Index (EPI) offers a broad measure of environmental health and ecosystem vitality, ranking countries based on factors such as air and water quality, biodiversity, and climate and energy policies. The EPI, as of 2022, identified Denmark, Luxembourg, and Switzerland as the leading cleanest countries in the world.But these rankings might vary if we look at more specific indicators. For example, according to IQAir World Report 2022, Iceland has the highest air quality score, closely followed by Australia and New Zealand. Contrarily, these countries' wastewater treatment efforts are ranked 25th, 10th, and 15th, respectively. Moreover, cultural norms and attitudes towards cleanliness, waste management, and littering impact a country's cleanliness. Therefore, assessing a country's cleanliness is a subjective and complex topic, heavily reliant on the specific dimensions evaluated.Sustainability-Focused Waste Management CompaniesForward-thinking waste management companies like Waste Management Inc (NYSE:WM), Waste Connections Inc (NYSE:WCN), and Republic Services Inc (NYSE:RSG) are continuously implementing efforts to make waste dumping sustainable. For instance, Waste Management Inc (NYSE:WM) has goals like greenhouse gas emissions reduction and responsible waste dumping. The company has started producing renewable fuels by capturing gases released from its landfills and converting it into low-carbon fuel that supports a portion of its fleet. Waste Management Inc (NYSE:WM) has a current market cap of $68.484 billion and it is one of the largest waste management companies in the USA. Story continuesMoreover, Waste Connections Inc (NYSE:WCN), the third-largest solid waste management company in North America, that boasts a current market cap of $36.346 billion, increased the use of robotics in its recycling facility and consistently recycles 50% of its collected waste. Waste Connections Inc (NYSE:WCN) also processes 50% of its leachate on-site and has completed the construction of two new leachate plants in 2022 to meet its groundwater safety goals. Arizona-based Republic Services Inc (NYSE:RSG) is also focused on responsible environmental solutions for the residential sector. For instance, Republic Services Inc (NYSE:RSG) has recorded a 9% reduction in its operational greenhouse gas emissions since 2017 and aims to drop this level to 10% by 2025. The company is also close to opening the country's first fully integrated plastic recycling facility in Las Vegas, named Polymer Center, by the end of this year, that'll aim to produce 100 million pounds of recycled plastic annually. Waste management companies are now focusing on recycling and clean energy sources more than ever. If you wish to be a part of these progressive mitigation efforts, read 11 Best Waste Management Stocks to Buy Now, and add more weight to your investment strategy. Which Is The No 1 Cleanest Country In The World?As per our recent analysis of multifaceted environmental parameters, Luxembourg is the cleanest country in the world in 2023. The country has exhibited an exemplary approach towards waste management, boasting an impressive recycling rate. Coupled with legislation and progressive public attitudes, this has facilitated a highly effective waste disposal system and minimized the country's environmental contamination. The wastewater treatment facilities in Luxembourg also display advanced technical acuity, achieving near-perfect filtration rates and significantly reducing aquatic pollution. This treatment proficiency and a remarkable level of infrastructure investment contribute to the nation's place among the top 10 cleanest countries in the world in 2023.Which Is The Cleanest Country In Asia?Japan's concerted efforts towards ecological sustainability confidently assert the country's distinction of being the cleanest country in Asia. Japan's initiatives focused on environmental preservation, particularly its commitment to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and developing renewable energy resources, have proven instrumental in setting new benchmarks for sustainable living. The country's environmentally-friendly policies are backed by robust infrastructure encouraging green practices and waste management.We have already covered 30 Least Polluted Countries in the World; give this detailed article a read to learn the planet's pollution dynamics. Which Is The Least Clean Country In The World?The Environmental Performance Index (EPI) 2022 report ranks India as the dirtiest country in the world, primarily due to its high population density, considerable vehicular congestion, and extensive biomass fuel usage. India's population growth, which is currently surpassing China, poses environmental challenges and calls for expansive mitigation efforts. For instance, urbanization and vehicular traffic explosion have badly impacted the country's air quality and propelled it to the bottom of the list. High emission levels from vehicles, combined with inadequate waste management, contribute to an alarming increase in air, water, and soil pollution. Additionally, India's reliance on biomass fuels, primarily in rural areas, further compounds the pollution problem. These fuels, including firewood, cow dung, and crop residues, emit substantial amounts of pollutants when burned. While India has tried to mitigate these issues, the magnitude of the challenges requires extensive environmental-friendly policies, justifying its ranking as the least clean country in the world per the EPI Report 2022.25 Cleanest Countries in the World in 202325 Cleanest Countries in the World in 2023Our Methodology To rank the 25 cleanest countries in the world in 2023, we relied on their air quality index, waste management system, and availability of wastewater treatment networks. To understand these crucial parameters, we referred to the Environmental Performance Index Report 2022 (collectively published by Yale and Columbia University), which analyzes 180 countries according to 40 environmental performance indicators. Our first step was to shortlist 25 countries with the best overall EPI score in 2022 (given that it is awarded based on extensive variables, these countries are doing well overall). Then, as solid waste management and wastewater treatment determine a country’s determination towards being ‘clean,’ we picked these two variables from the EPI Report and shortlisted 25 countries with the highest score in these categories. The report has awarded wastewater treatment scores to countries depending on what percentage of a nation’s wastewater undergoes at least some kind of treatment. For example, if a country’s whole population is connected to a sewerage system and all of the collected wastewater is treated, its score will be 100%. Similarly, the EPI Index measures a country’s waste management system according to its efforts to limit solid waste, recycling rates, and oceanic plastic pollution. So if a nation’s solid waste management score is 79%, it indicates its overall performance in these criteria collectively. For our 3rd key metric, i.e., air quality index, we referred to the IQAir World Air Quality Report 2022, which scores countries based on PM2.5 ranking. PM2.5 refers to atmospheric particulate matter (PM) with a diameter of less than 2.5 micrometers. So if a place’s air has particulate matter between 0-12 μg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter), it is considered good. Likewise, AQI of 12.1-34.5 μg/m³ is moderate, while a μg/m³ score of 55.5-150.4 is unhealthy. In short, the lower the 2.5PM rating, the better a country’s air quality will be.After listing these three variables individually for the top 25 countries, we averaged their scores to get composite rankings to present a broader perspective of their cleanliness levels. Based on our findings, here are the 25 cleanest countries in the world in 2023: 25. Cyprus Composite Ranking: 25 Air Quality PM2.5 concentration (μg/m³): 15.6 Waste Management Score: 58.9%  Wastewater Treatment Score: 50%  Our list of cleanest countries in the world in 2023 starts with Cyprus, owing to its moderate wastewater treatment system and solid waste management efforts. Although the country's air quality index is 15.6 (PM2.5 μg/m³ being the best score), its moderate waste system is commendable. Also, stringent regulations on emissions combined with a transition towards renewable energy have significantly improved the country's air quality.24. Croatia Composite Ranking: 24 Air Quality PM2.5 concentration (μg/m³): 23.5  Waste Management Score: 55.3%  Wastewater Treatment Score: 69% When tested on indicators like environmental performance and eco-friendly waste mitigation, Croatia finds a place amongst the cleanest countries in 2023. The country's stellar environmental status is a result of rigorous national policies that promote renewable energy, waste management, and biodiversity conservation. UNESCO's sustainability index also applauds Croatia's dedication to maintaining pristine ecosystems.23. Italy Composite Ranking: 23 Air Quality PM2.5 concentration (μg/m³): 18.9  Waste Management Score: 60.6%  Wastewater Treatment Score: 58.8%Italy is also one of the world's cleanest countries in 2023, according to the Environmental Performance Index (EPI). column4: A Look At The Fair Value Of Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM)
column10: [Key InsightsThe projected fair value for Waste Management is US$151 based on 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to EquityWith US$171 share price, Waste Management appears to be trading close to its estimated fair value Analyst price target for WM is US$175, which is 16% above our fair value estimateHow far off is Waste Management, Inc. (NYSE:WM) from its intrinsic value? Using the most recent financial data, we'll take a look at whether the stock is fairly priced by taking the forecast future cash flows of the company and discounting them back to today's value. We will take advantage of the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model for this purpose. It may sound complicated, but actually it is quite simple!We generally believe that a company's value is the present value of all of the cash it will generate in the future. However, a DCF is just one valuation metric among many, and it is not without flaws. For those who are keen learners of equity analysis, the Simply Wall St analysis model here may be something of interest to you. Check out our latest analysis for Waste Management The ModelWe are going to use a two-stage DCF model, which, as the name states, takes into account two stages of growth. The first stage is generally a higher growth period which levels off heading towards the terminal value, captured in the second 'steady growth' period. To start off with, we need to estimate the next ten years of cash flows. Where possible we use analyst estimates, but when these aren't available we extrapolate the previous free cash flow (FCF) from the last estimate or reported value. We assume companies with shrinking free cash flow will slow their rate of shrinkage, and that companies with growing free cash flow will see their growth rate slow, over this period. We do this to reflect that growth tends to slow more in the early years than it does in later years.A DCF is all about the idea that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today, so we discount the value of these future cash flows to their estimated value in today's dollars:Story continues10-year free cash flow (FCF) estimate2024202520262027202820292030203120322033 Levered FCF ($, Millions) US$2.42bUS$3.02bUS$3.45bUS$3.68bUS$3.86bUS$4.02bUS$4.16bUS$4.29bUS$4.41bUS$4.52bGrowth Rate Estimate SourceAnalyst x14Analyst x7Analyst x3Analyst x3Est @ 4.89%Est @ 4.05%Est @ 3.47%Est @ 3.06%Est @ 2.78%Est @ 2.58% Present Value ($, Millions) Discounted @ 7.9% US$2.2kUS$2.6kUS$2.7kUS$2.7kUS$2.6kUS$2.5kUS$2.4kUS$2.3kUS$2.2kUS$2.1k("Est" = FCF growth rate estimated by Simply Wall St)Present Value of 10-year Cash Flow (PVCF) = US$25bAfter calculating the present value of future cash flows in the initial 10-year period, we need to calculate the Terminal Value, which accounts for all future cash flows beyond the first stage. For a number of reasons a very conservative growth rate is used that cannot exceed that of a country's GDP growth. In this case we have used the 5-year average of the 10-year government bond yield (2.1%) to estimate future growth. In the same way as with the 10-year 'growth' period, we discount future cash flows to today's value, using a cost of equity of 7.9%.Terminal Value (TV)= FCF2033 × (1 + g) ÷ (r – g) = US$4.5b× (1 + 2.1%) ÷ (7.9%– 2.1%) = US$79bPresent Value of Terminal Value (PVTV)= TV / (1 + r)10= US$79b÷ ( 1 + 7.9%)10= US$37bThe total value, or equity value, is then the sum of the present value of the future cash flows, which in this case is US$61b. The last step is to then divide the equity value by the number of shares outstanding. Relative to the current share price of US$171, the company appears around fair value at the time of writing. Remember though, that this is just an approximate valuation, and like any complex formula - garbage in, garbage out.dcfThe AssumptionsNow the most important inputs to a discounted cash flow are the discount rate, and of course, the actual cash flows. If you don't agree with these result, have a go at the calculation yourself and play with the assumptions. The DCF also does not consider the possible cyclicality of an industry, or a company's future capital requirements, so it does not give a full picture of a company's potential performance. Given that we are looking at Waste Management as potential shareholders, the cost of equity is used as the discount rate, rather than the cost of capital (or weighted average cost of capital, WACC) which accounts for debt. In this calculation we've used 7.9%, which is based on a levered beta of 0.981. Beta is a measure of a stock's volatility, compared to the market as a whole. We get our beta from the industry average beta of globally comparable companies, with an imposed limit between 0.8 and 2.0, which is a reasonable range for a stable business.SWOT Analysis for Waste ManagementStrengthEarnings growth over the past year exceeded the industry.Debt is well covered by earnings and cashflows.Dividends are covered by earnings and cash flows.WeaknessDividend is low compared to the top 25% of dividend payers in the Commercial Services market.OpportunityAnnual earnings are forecast to grow for the next 3 years.Good value based on P/E ratio compared to estimated Fair P/E ratio.ThreatAnnual earnings are forecast to grow slower than the American market.Moving On:Although the valuation of a company is important, it is only one of many factors that you need to assess for a company. DCF models are not the be-all and end-all of investment valuation. Instead the best use for a DCF model is to test certain assumptions and theories to see if they would lead to the company being undervalued or overvalued. If a company grows at a different rate, or if its cost of equity or risk free rate changes sharply, the output can look very different. column4: 7 Stocks to Buy Now if You Still Think a Recession Is Ahead
column10: [Preparing for a recession at this juncture seems a ridiculous concept at this juncture. As CNBC pointed out late last week, the Federal Reserve’s key inflation measure showed that prices increased by just 0.3% in May, favorably below expectations. Put another way, disinflation is occurring which means that recession-proof stocks are only for worrywarts, right?Well, maybe not. While the inflation data is encouraging, it’s also worth pointing out that the U.S. Supreme Court struck down President Biden’s plan to forgive student debt. That will likely weigh on discretionary retail sectors as affected individuals face a harsh reality check. Thus, it’s still a good idea to at least consider safe stocks in a recession.Also, credit card debt hit a record high, implying that the Covid-19 pandemic failed to teach financial prudence. Should circumstances go awry, many if not most households lack the wherewithal to navigate effectively. Therefore, the below recession stocks to buy remain relevant despite the latest headline numbers.InvestorPlace - Stock Market News, Stock Advice & Trading TipsRecession-Proof Stocks: Waste Management (WM)man's hand holding wads of cash. stocks to buy. In contrast, the underlying sector median stat is 16.63 times. As a major player in the supermarket segment, Kroger stands to benefit from the trade-down effect. This concept involves consumers trading down their common purchases for cheaper alternatives (rather than going cold turkey). By logical deduction, Kroger represents a trade-down for consumers who previously went out to restaurants or ordered food deliveries.Financially, Kroger presents a very intriguing argument for investing during a recession. Sure, the company only features a trailing-year net margin of 1.71%, which is slightly worse than the sector median of 1.82%. At the same time, Kroger carries a three-year revenue growth rate of 10.3%, outpacing nearly 70% of sector rivals.Most enticingly, the market prices KR at a forward multiple of 10.44. As a discount to projected earnings, Kroger ranks better than 83.08% of enterprises in the defensive retail space. Also, it trades at 0.23 times trailing sales, favorably below 69.9% of its peers. Thus, it’s one of the safe stocks in recession.Five Below (FIVE)A person draws a stock chart on a chalkboard.Source: Zurijeta / Shutterstock.comWhile I’m a big fan of discount dollar stores as a frontline strategy for recession-proof stocks, they can also be problematic. Let’s face reality: dollar stores tend to be grimy affairs that might not attract customers during non-recession years. Fortunately, Five Below (NASDAQ:FIVE) fills a nice niche in the discount retail space.Offering products priced mostly at five bucks but also select products that run to $25, Five Below delivers a bargain and a touch of class.
